# Judith Chapter 14 — Disagreement Log

**Date:** 2026-03-17
**Chapter:** Judith 14 (19 verses)
**Theme:** Judith's tactical plan; Achior's conversion; discovery of Holofernes' body

---

## Disagreement Count: 18

---

### Disagreement 1 — Verse 2: Tactical instruction phrasing

**EMET:** "each one of you shall take up his weapons of war and every able-bodied man shall go out of the city"
**LOGOS:** "let every man take up his weapons of war, and let every able-bodied man march out"
**PNEUMA:** "every man arms himself and marches out — every last able-bodied man"

**Issue:** PNEUMA adds "every last" — not in the text. LOGOS/EMET render more literally.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Let every man take up his weapons of war, and let every able-bodied man march out." LOGOS preferred.

---

### Disagreement 2 — Verse 2: "do not go down" — emphasis

**EMET:** "but do not go down"
**LOGOS:** "but do not go down"
**PNEUMA:** "But don't go down"

**Issue:** Minor register. PNEUMA's contraction appropriate for dynamic style but not for consensus.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "But do not go down."

---

### Disagreement 3 — Verse 3: "rouse" vs. "wake" vs. "go to"

**EMET:** "rouse the commanders of the Assyrian army"
**LOGOS:** "wake the officers"
**PNEUMA:** "rouse their officers"

**Issue:** Greek diegeirousin — to rouse/wake. "Rouse" is slightly stronger than "wake" and carries military connotation.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Rouse the officers of the Assyrian army."

---

### Disagreement 4 — Verse 4: "cut them down in their paths" vs. "in their tracks"

**EMET:** "cut them down in their paths"
**LOGOS:** "cut them down in their tracks"
**PNEUMA:** "Cut them down where they stand"

**Issue:** "In their paths" (en tais hodois autōn) is literal. "In their tracks" is idiomatic English equivalent. PNEUMA's "where they stand" is less accurate (they are fleeing).
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Cut them down in their tracks" — natural English idiom that accurately captures fleeing enemies being overtaken.

---

### Disagreement 5 — Verse 5: "treated with contempt" vs. "scorned"

**EMET:** "who treated the house of Israel with contempt"
**LOGOS:** "who treated the house of Israel with contempt"
**PNEUMA:** "who scorned the house of Israel"

**Issue:** Minor — "contempt" vs. "scorned." Greek katephronēsen — to despise/treat with contempt.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Who treated the house of Israel with contempt" — the phrase is more measured and formal.

---

### Disagreement 6 — Verse 6: Achior's response — fainting

**EMET:** "he fell on his face and his spirit left him"
**LOGOS:** "he fell on his face and his spirit failed him"
**PNEUMA:** "he dropped to the ground. His spirit left him."

**Issue:** "His spirit left him" vs. "his spirit failed him" — Greek exepsychē. "Failed" suggests the spirit remained but weakened; "left" is more literally the Greek (ex + psychē = out + spirit). However, he is clearly not dead.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "He fell on his face and his spirit failed him" — "failed" better captures a temporary loss of consciousness without implying death.

---

### Disagreement 7 — Verse 7: "filled with dread" vs. "dismayed" vs. "struck with awe"

**EMET:** "those who hear your name will be dismayed"
**LOGOS:** "all who hear your name will be filled with dread"
**PNEUMA:** "everyone who hears your name will be struck with awe"

**Issue:** Greek ptooēthēsontai — to be terrified/struck with sudden fear. "Dismayed" (EMET) is too mild. "Awe" (PNEUMA) is too positive. "Filled with dread" (LOGOS) is most accurate.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "All who hear your name will be filled with dread."

---

### Disagreement 8 — Verse 8: How Judith tells her story

**EMET:** "Judith told him all the things she had done, in the presence of all the people"
**LOGOS:** "Judith told him, in the hearing of all the people, everything she had done"
**PNEUMA:** "Judith told him everything. When she finished, the crowd erupted with a roar"

**Issue:** PNEUMA compresses and loses "in the presence of all the people" as a structural element. The public nature of Judith's testimony is important — it is not a private report.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Judith told him, in the hearing of all the people, everything she had done."

---

### Disagreement 9 — Verse 9: Achior's conversion — "incorporated"

**EMET:** "he was added to the house of Israel"
**LOGOS:** "he was incorporated into the house of Israel"
**PNEUMA:** "he became part of the house of Israel"

**Issue:** Greek prosetethe eis ton oikon Israēl — "he was added/joined to the house of Israel." "Incorporated" (LOGOS) is more formal and precise; "became part of" (PNEUMA) is loose.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "He was incorporated into the house of Israel" — the formal-legal sense of being added to a covenant community fits the action of circumcision.

---

### Disagreement 10 — Verse 9: "and so it has remained to this day"

**EMET:** "even to this day"
**LOGOS:** "and so it has remained to this day"
**PNEUMA:** "And so it has remained to this day"

**Issue:** The phrase heos tēs hēmeras tautēs — "until this day." LOGOS/PNEUMA expand slightly to "has remained"; EMET is more literal with "even to this day."
**SOPHIA ruling:** "And so it has remained to this day" — the slight expansion makes the continuing reality clearer in English.

---

### Disagreement 11 — Verse 10: Timing of the display

**EMET:** "as soon as the morning appeared"
**LOGOS:** "as soon as morning dawned"
**PNEUMA:** "At first light"

**Issue:** Greek hama tō prōi — "as soon as it was morning." "At first light" (PNEUMA) is slightly more evocative; "as soon as morning dawned" (LOGOS) is precise.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "As soon as morning dawned" — literal and natural.

---

### Disagreement 12 — Verse 11: Chain of command description

**EMET:** "they sent word to their commanders, and those went to the generals and the captains and to every ruler"
**LOGOS:** "they sent word to their commanders, who in turn went to the generals, the captains, and all the officers"
**PNEUMA:** "Word went up the chain of command — to the commanders, the generals, the captains, all the officers"

**Issue:** PNEUMA's "chain of command" is an interpretive phrase not in the text. LOGOS uses the relative clause structure.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "They sent word to their commanders, who in turn went to the generals, the captains, and all the officers."

---

### Disagreement 13 — Verse 12: "the slaves" — ironic use

**EMET:** "for the slaves have dared to come down against us for battle"
**LOGOS:** "for the slaves have dared to march down against us to give battle"
**PNEUMA:** "Those slaves have had the nerve to come down against us"

**Issue:** "Dared" vs. "had the nerve" — PNEUMA's colloquialism is appropriate for dynamic but not for consensus. "For battle" vs. "to give battle" — minor.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "For the slaves have dared to march down against us to give battle." "March" is more militarily precise.

---

### Disagreement 14 — Verse 13: Bagoas' assumption

**EMET:** "for he supposed he was sleeping with Judith"
**LOGOS:** "supposing that Holofernes was sleeping with Judith"
**PNEUMA:** "He assumed Holofernes was sleeping with Judith."

**Issue:** LOGOS explicitly names Holofernes as the subject for clarity; EMET's pronoun is ambiguous in English.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Supposing that Holofernes was sleeping with Judith" — explicit subject needed.

---

### Disagreement 15 — Verse 14: Discovery of the body — rendering

**EMET:** "found him thrown on the threshold, dead, with his head taken from him"
**LOGOS:** "found him thrown on the threshold, dead, his head taken from him"
**PNEUMA:** "He was thrown on the threshold. Dead. Without his head."

**Issue:** PNEUMA breaks the finding into three staccato sentences — powerful as dramatic prose but departs from the single Greek clause. EMET/LOGOS preserve the structure while adding weight.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Found him thrown on the threshold, dead, with his head taken from him." The single clause with its three heavy elements (thrown, dead, headless) delivers the impact through accumulation.

---

### Disagreement 16 — Verse 15: Bagoas' lamentation

**EMET:** "he cried out with a loud voice and wept and groaned and shouted and tore his garments"
**LOGOS:** "He cried out with a loud voice and wept and moaned and shouted and tore his garments"
**PNEUMA:** "Bagoas let out a scream. He wept. He groaned. He kept shouting. He tore his clothes apart."

**Issue:** The Greek lists five actions in sequence. PNEUMA breaks them into five short sentences for effect; EMET/LOGOS maintain the list structure which has its own accumulative horror. "Groaned" vs. "moaned" — Greek estenazen = to groan/sigh deeply.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "He cried out with a loud voice and wept and moaned and shouted and tore his garments." The list form is retained — the accumulation in the original is an effect the author intended.

---

### Disagreement 17 — Verse 17: Bagoas' announcement — "One Hebrew woman"

**EMET:** "One Hebrew woman has brought disgrace upon the house of King Nebuchadnezzar"
**LOGOS:** "One Hebrew woman has brought disgrace upon the house of King Nebuchadnezzar"
**PNEUMA:** "One Hebrew woman — one woman — has shamed the entire house of King Nebuchadnezzar"

**Issue:** PNEUMA doubles "one woman" for emphasis — a reasonable rhetorical expansion but not in the text. All agree on "disgrace" vs. "shamed."
**SOPHIA ruling:** "One Hebrew woman has brought disgrace upon the house of King Nebuchadnezzar." The single phrase is powerful enough without doubling.

---

### Disagreement 18 — Verse 18: Nature of the distress

**EMET:** "an excessive distress fell upon them"
**LOGOS:** "a terrible dread came over them"
**PNEUMA:** "A terror came over them unlike anything they had felt"

**Issue:** Greek kataplexis sphodra — "a great/excessive consternation/terror." EMET's "excessive distress" is literal but awkward in English. LOGOS' "terrible dread" is effective. PNEUMA's "unlike anything they had felt" is an addition.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "A terrible dread came over them" — strong, accurate, and idiomatic.

---

## Summary

Total disagreements: 18
Theologically significant: v. 9 (Achior's conversion — an Ammonite joining Israel); v. 13 (Bagoas' devastating irony)
Narratively significant: v. 14 (discovery of the body — three-element climax)
Structural: Judith's speech in vv. 1-5 sets the military strategy; Achior's conversion (vv. 6-9) provides the theological response; the Assyrian discovery (vv. 10-19) begins the collapse.
